buildUp: Start with the seal: a soft silicone tip closes the ear canal, so a tiny speaker driver can make deep bass and outside sound is partly blocked.
To cancel the noise that still leaks in, each bud gets outer microphones to hear the world and a chip fast enough to produce the opposite wave in real time.
With no wire to the phone, music must come by Bluetooth, so each bud needs a radio and an antenna, which runs down the stem to keep it clear of your head.
Your mouth is several centimetres from your ear, so the stem reaches down to put a voice microphone closer to it, helped by a motion sensor that feels your jaw vibrate when you speak.
The battery that fits is tiny, so the buds sleep when out of your ears, and the case becomes a pocket charger with a battery about ten times bigger.
Magnets in the case pull each bud onto charging contacts so they always land in the right place, and the case itself charges by USB-C or a wireless pad.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Seal the ear canal and treat it as a tiny pressure chamber, so a speaker smaller than a fingernail can make deep bass and outside noise is already partly blocked. Then use microphones and a fast chip to cancel the noise that still gets through, and let the case carry the big battery so the buds only need enough for a few hours.

hardParts.title: Cancelling noise in real time
hardParts.why: The chip has to hear the noise, work out the opposite wave and play it within a fraction of a millisecond, while also keeping your music untouched and adjusting as the fit in your ear shifts. An inner microphone listens to what actually reaches your eardrum so the bud can correct itself continuously.

hardParts.title: A radio link that survives your head
hardParts.why: Bluetooth uses waves at about 2.4 GHz, the same band microwave ovens use, and the water in your body absorbs them strongly. The link has to reach from your phone to both ears, round or through your head, and keep left and right in step to within microseconds, all on a few milliwatts.

hardParts.title: Fitting it all into 5 grams
hardParts.why: A speaker, battery, radio, processor, several microphones and sensors have to fit in a shell moulded to about a tenth of a millimetre, shaped to sit comfortably in ears that vary widely. Every gram added makes the bud more likely to fall out.

principles.explanation: In a sealed ear canal even a tiny speaker movement makes a strong pressure change, so a small driver can produce deep bass as long as the tip seals. Your ear canal is about 25 mm long and 7 mm across, holding only about 1 cubic centimetre of air. In open air, a small speaker playing bass just sloshes air around its edges, but in a sealed space it squeezes the air like pushing a syringe with your thumb over the end. So a driver just 6 to 11 mm across is enough, but the bass vanishes the moment the tip stops sealing.
principles.title: A sealed ear is a tiny pressure chamber

principles.explanation: A sound wave that's exactly opposite to the noise cancels it, so the bud listens to the noise around you and plays its mirror image alongside your music. Sound is a wave of pressure going up and down. Where the noise pushes the pressure up, the mirror wave pulls it down, so the two add up to nearly nothing. The bud's outer microphone hears noise coming, the chip calculates the opposite wave, and the speaker plays it. It works best on steady, low sounds such as engine rumble, which change slowly and are easy to predict.
principles.title: Two waves can cancel

principles.explanation: Even a tiny delay knocks the anti-noise out of step with high pitches, so noise cancelling is strongest at low pitches and the seal has to block the higher ones. The anti-noise has to be in step with the noise. A delay of half a millisecond barely matters for a 100 Hz hum, whose wave takes 10 milliseconds to repeat, but at 1,000 Hz it's half a whole cycle, so the anti-noise would arrive in step with the noise and make it louder.
principles.title: Timing is everything

principles.explanation: A bud's battery is so small that the whole bud must average only a few tens of milliwatts, so every part is chosen and run to sip power. A bud's battery holds roughly 50 mAh at 3.7 V, about 0.19 watt-hours, less than a fiftieth of a phone battery. Playing for about 5 to 6 hours on that means around 30 to 40 milliwatts, shared between the radio, the chip and the speaker. The buds also sleep the moment their skin sensor says they're out of your ear.
principles.title: A few milliwatts at a time

firstPrinciples.problem: Deliver rich, deep sound straight into your ears with no wires at all, block out the noise around you, pick up your voice clearly on calls and last for hours, all from something weighing about 5 grams that stays comfortably in your ear. Deep bass normally needs a big speaker, silence normally needs thick ear muffs, and hours of playback normally needs a big battery, and none of those fit.

questions.answer: A tip that doesn't seal lets air leak out round the edges. The tiny speaker can no longer pressurise the closed ear canal, and in open air it's far too small to push enough air for deep notes.
questions.question: Why does the bass disappear if the ear tip is the wrong size?

questions.answer: Engine rumble is low and steady, so the anti-noise can stay in step with it. A baby's cry is higher and keeps changing, and at higher pitches any tiny delay puts the anti-noise out of step, so the seal has to do most of the blocking.
questions.question: Why do noise-cancelling earbuds silence an aircraft engine better than a crying baby?

questions.answer: A bigger battery would make them heavier and larger, so they'd be uncomfortable and fall out more easily. Short top-ups in the case give you hours more listening without adding weight to your ears.
questions.question: Why not just give the buds bigger batteries instead of a charging case?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: Earbuds are less a tiny speaker than a tiny real-time sound computer. By sealing the ear and then constantly listening both outside and inside it, they shape the sound reaching your eardrum, cancelling noise, letting in voices when you want, and adjusting to your ear, in something weighing about as much as a sheet of printer paper.

name: Wireless Earbuds
overview:
Wireless earbuds are some of the most densely packed things people own. Each bud weighs about 5 grams, yet holds a speaker, a rechargeable battery, a Bluetooth radio, a processor, several microphones and sensors that know when it's in your ear. Nothing connects the two buds or ties them to your phone: music arrives over Bluetooth, and the buds keep each other in sync.

The trick that makes them sound bigger than they are is the seal. A soft silicone tip closes off your ear canal, so the tiny speaker only has to move a little air to make deep bass. The seal also blocks outside sound, and noise cancelling does the rest: microphones listen to the world outside, and the chip plays back the exact opposite sound wave, hundreds of thousands of times a second, so the noise cancels out before it reaches your eardrum.

The batteries in the buds only last a few hours, so the case carries a much bigger battery. Drop the buds in and magnets pull them onto metal contacts that charge them; the case itself charges over USB-C or by lying on a wireless charging pad.

parts.description: Soft silicone tip that seals the ear canal, for deep bass and to block outside noise; it clicks off to swap sizes.

details.didYouKnow: Many earbud apps can play a short test tone and measure it with the inside microphone to check whether the seal is good, telling you to try a different tip size if sound is leaking out.
details.howItWorks: The tip squashes gently against the walls of your ear canal and forms an airtight seal. That seal traps the low-frequency pressure waves from the driver so bass stays full, and it blocks a good share of higher-pitched outside noise before the electronics even get involved. A small plastic collar inside the tip clips onto the nozzle of the inner shell so it stays put but can be swapped.
keyNumbers: Usually supplied in about 3 to 4 sizes
Each tip weighs well under 1 g
A good seal can cut outside noise by roughly 15 to 25 dB on its own
details.madeOf: Soft medical-grade silicone over a stiffer plastic clip ring. Silicone is comfortable against skin for hours, does not irritate most people, and springs back to shape after being squeezed thousands of times.

parts.name: Left ear tip

parts.description: Half of the bud that faces your ear, with the sound outlet, a vent and a window for the skin sensor.

details.didYouKnow: The two shell halves are usually welded or glued shut rather than screwed together, which is why earbuds are notoriously hard to open for repair.
details.howItWorks: The inner shell forms the sealed back chamber behind the driver and the angled nozzle that steers sound into the ear canal. A tiny vent lets air pressure equalise, which avoids the blocked-ear feeling and stops your footsteps thudding through the bud. It also holds the window for the skin sensor and the opening for the inward-facing microphone.
keyNumbers: Whole bud weighs about 5 g
Wall thickness typically under 1 mm
Vent opening only a fraction of a millimetre across
details.madeOf: A hard, glossy engineering plastic such as polycarbonate, moulded to tight tolerances. Plastic lets radio signals pass, is light, and can be shaped into the curved, ear-friendly form in one moulding.

parts.name: Left inner shell

parts.description: Sensor that tells skin from a pocket or a table, so music pauses the moment you take the bud out.

details.didYouKnow: Early wireless earbuds relied on simple light-based proximity sensors, which could be fooled by anything close and dark; sensing skin itself makes in-ear detection far more reliable.
details.howItWorks: The sensor looks through a small window in the inner shell and checks whether something with the properties of skin is pressing against it. Simple proximity sensors could be fooled by a pocket lining or a desk, so the processor combines its reading with motion data before deciding the bud is really in an ear. When it decides the bud has come out, it tells the phone to pause playback.
keyNumbers: Sensor chip only a few millimetres across
Reacts in well under 1 second
Uses roughly microwatts to milliwatts of power
details.madeOf: A tiny sensor chip, typically optical or capacitive, behind a clear or tinted plastic window. The window is designed to pass the sensor's signal while blending in with the glossy shell.

parts.name: Left skin sensor

parts.description: Tiny microphone in the sound outlet that listens to what's actually reaching your ear, so noise cancelling can correct what it missed.

details.didYouKnow: Listening inside the ear also lets some buds check their own seal: they play a short sound when you put them in and measure how it comes back, then adjust the bass to suit your ear.
details.howItWorks: The outward-facing microphones hear noise before it arrives, but they can't know how the bud is sitting in your ear. This second microphone sits between the speaker and your eardrum and hears what's actually left over. The chip compares it with what it meant to play and corrects the difference many thousands of times a second.
keyNumbers: About the size of a grain of rice or smaller
Part of a correction loop running thousands of times a second
details.madeOf: A MEMS microphone: a tiny silicon membrane etched from a chip, in a small metal can that shields it from radio interference, on a flexible circuit.

parts.name: Left inner microphone

parts.description: Tiny speaker with a light diaphragm and a magnet, pointed straight down the ear canal.

details.didYouKnow: The moving-coil loudspeaker was patented in the 1920s, and the same basic idea now works at a scale small enough to hide in a fingertip-sized earbud.
details.howItWorks: This is a dynamic driver: a coil of very fine wire is glued to the back of a thin diaphragm and sits in the gap of a powerful magnet. When the amplifier sends current through the coil it is pushed and pulled in the magnetic field, moving the diaphragm and the air in front of it. The noise-cancelling engine sends its anti-noise through this same driver, mixed in with your music.
keyNumbers: Diaphragm roughly 6 to 11 mm across
Covers roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, the range of human hearing
Diaphragm moves only fractions of a millimetre
details.madeOf: A thin polymer diaphragm, a copper or copper-clad aluminium voice coil and a small neodymium magnet in a plastic frame. Neodymium gives a strong magnetic field from a magnet that weighs only a fraction of a gram.

parts.name: Left speaker driver

parts.description: Folded circuit board with the Bluetooth radio, audio processor and noise-cancelling engine in one package.

details.didYouKnow: Bluetooth is named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king, and its logo combines the runes for his initials H and B.
details.howItWorks: The board carries a system-in-package that combines a Bluetooth radio, a processor, memory and audio converters. It decodes the compressed music stream from your phone, turns it into an analogue signal for the driver, and runs the noise-cancelling maths hundreds of thousands of times a second using the microphones. It also reads the sensors, manages the battery and keeps the two buds in sync.
keyNumbers: Bluetooth radio works at about 2.4 GHz
Typically supports Bluetooth 5 or later
Whole package only about the size of a fingernail
details.madeOf: Silicon chips stacked and sealed in an epoxy package on a multilayer circuit board, part of which is flexible so it can fold into the bud's curved shape. Folding lets one board snake around the battery and driver.

parts.name: Left audio chip & board

parts.description: Button-shaped lithium-ion cell that runs the bud for several hours between visits to the case.

details.didYouKnow: Lithium-ion batteries went on sale in 1991, and three of the scientists who developed them shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
details.howItWorks: The cell stores energy as lithium ions packed between layers of carbon in one electrode. While the bud plays music the ions travel through the electrolyte to the metal-oxide electrode, releasing electrons through the circuit to power the chip, driver and sensors. A protection circuit on the board stops it from being overcharged or drained too far.
keyNumbers: Capacity roughly 40 to 60 mAh
Nominal voltage about 3.7 V
Roughly 5 to 6 hours of listening per charge
details.madeOf: A graphite anode, a lithium metal-oxide cathode and a liquid or gel electrolyte, all sealed in a small stainless steel can. The steel case is strong enough to resist swelling and seals out moisture.

parts.name: Left battery

parts.description: Glossy outer half of the bud, with mesh-covered openings for the outward-facing microphones.

details.didYouKnow: Earbud shells are usually shaped using scans of thousands of ears, because ear shapes vary so much that no single design fits everyone perfectly.
details.howItWorks: The outer shell closes the back of the bud and is the part people see when you wear it. Its mesh-covered openings feed outside sound to the feedforward microphone, and its shape is tuned so wind flowing past causes as little rumble as possible. Because it is plastic, Bluetooth signals pass straight through it to the antenna.
keyNumbers: Bud about 30 mm tall including the stem
Typically rated around IPX4 for sweat and splashes
Shell plus all internals about 5 g
details.madeOf: Glossy polycarbonate or a similar plastic, often with a hard-wearing coating. Plastic keeps weight down and, unlike metal, does not block radio signals.

parts.name: Left outer shell

parts.description: Acoustic mesh over the microphone that listens to outside noise for noise cancelling and transparency mode.

details.didYouKnow: The idea of cancelling noise with an opposite sound wave was patented by the German physicist Paul Lueg in the 1930s, decades before electronics were small enough to do it in an earbud.
details.howItWorks: The mesh sits over the outward-facing microphone port and lets sound through while keeping out dust, earwax and sweat. Its fine weave also slows down gusts of air, which reduces the roar of wind noise in the microphone. That microphone hears outside noise a split second before it reaches your eardrum, giving the processor time to create the matching anti-noise.
keyNumbers: Holes typically tens of micrometres wide
Mesh roughly 0.1 mm thick
Active noise cancelling works best below roughly 1 kHz
details.madeOf: Very fine woven stainless steel or polymer mesh, often with a water-repellent coating. Steel mesh is strong for its thinness and does not sag or clog easily.

parts.name: Left outer microphone mesh

parts.description: Stem that carries the antenna, microphones and the squeeze control, and points the voice mic toward your mouth.

details.didYouKnow: Stems were once mocked as looking odd, but they solve a real engineering problem: a microphone closer to your mouth and an antenna further from your head both work noticeably better.
details.howItWorks: The stem is the long body that hangs below the ear and acts as a structural spine for the antenna, the squeeze sensor and the voice microphone. Keeping these parts in the stem moves them away from your head, which would otherwise soak up radio signals and muffle your voice. It also gives you something to grip when taking the bud out.
keyNumbers: Stem typically about 15 to 20 mm long
Only a few millimetres thick
Holds at least 3 separate components
details.madeOf: The same moulded plastic as the shell, often formed in one piece with the outer half. Plastic keeps the antenna's signals unblocked and keeps the long stem light so the bud does not tip out of your ear.

parts.name: Left stem

parts.description: Pressure sensor in the flat of the stem: squeeze to play, pause, skip or switch noise modes.

details.didYouKnow: Using squeezes instead of taps means you do not push the bud deeper into your ear to control it, which many people find more comfortable.
details.howItWorks: When you pinch the flat of the stem, the plastic flexes by a tiny amount and the sensor measures that change in pressure. The processor looks at how hard and how long you squeezed, so one press can mean play or pause, two can skip and a long press can switch noise modes. A short click sound in the driver confirms the press, since there is no physical button to feel.
keyNumbers: Detects stem flex of only micrometres
Recognises up to 4 gestures: single, double and triple squeezes and a long press
Sensor element well under 1 mm thick
details.madeOf: A thin force or strain-sensing element on a flexible circuit, pressed against the inside of the stem wall. Measuring flex through a sealed wall means there is no gap for water or sweat to get in.

parts.name: Left squeeze sensor

parts.description: Thin conductor running down the stem, as far from your head as possible, for a steadier Bluetooth link.

details.didYouKnow: Microwave ovens and Wi-Fi share the same 2.4 GHz band, which is why some earbuds stutter briefly when you stand right beside a running microwave.
details.howItWorks: The antenna turns electrical signals from the radio into 2.4 GHz radio waves and back again. Its length is tuned to a fraction of the wavelength so it resonates efficiently, and running it down the stem keeps it clear of your head, which is mostly water and absorbs these frequencies. Each bud also uses its antenna to talk to the other bud across your head.
keyNumbers: 2.4 GHz radio waves are about 12.5 cm long
Antenna typically a quarter-wavelength or less, around 3 cm
Bluetooth range typically about 10 m
details.madeOf: A thin copper trace or stamped copper strip, sometimes printed directly onto a plastic part. Copper conducts very well, so little signal is lost as heat.

parts.name: Left antenna

parts.description: Microphone at the tip of the stem that picks up your voice for calls, helped by a bone-motion sensor.

details.didYouKnow: MEMS microphones are made with the same techniques used to make computer chips, so billions are produced every year for phones, laptops and earbuds.
details.howItWorks: This microphone sits at the bottom of the stem, the closest point to your mouth. It works together with the outer microphone to form a beam that favours sound coming from below and ignores noise from the sides. A motion sensor that feels your jaw vibrate while you talk tells the processor when it is really you speaking.
keyNumbers: Microphone chip roughly 3 mm long
Membrane only about a micrometre thick
Wideband call audio covers roughly 50 Hz to 7 kHz
details.madeOf: A MEMS microphone: a tiny silicon chip with a flexible membrane etched into it, inside a small metal can. MEMS microphones are tiny, robust and can be soldered automatically onto circuit boards.

parts.name: Left voice microphone

parts.description: Gold-plated contacts at the end of the stem that touch matching pins in the case to charge.

details.didYouKnow: If a bud stops charging, the most common cause is simply grime on the contacts, and a gentle wipe with a dry cloth often fixes it.
details.howItWorks: When the bud drops into its well, these contacts land on spring-loaded pins in the case and close the charging circuit. The same contacts carry small data signals so the case can tell the bud is home and read its battery level. Magnets in the case hold the bud down so the contacts press firmly together.
keyNumbers: Gold plating typically under 1 micrometre thick
Charging current roughly tens of milliamps
Usually 2 or more contact points per bud
details.madeOf: A thin layer of gold plated over a base metal such as nickel or copper. Gold does not tarnish, so sweat and skin oils will not build up a resistive layer that stops charging.

parts.name: Left charging contacts

parts.description: Soft silicone tip that seals the ear canal, for deep bass and to block outside noise; it clicks off to swap sizes.

details.didYouKnow: It is perfectly normal for your left and right ears to need different tip sizes; many people find the best seal with a mismatched pair.
details.howItWorks: Because your two ear canals are rarely exactly the same shape, the right tip is chosen independently and you can wear a different size on each side. Once fitted, the tip acts as passive hearing protection, blocking higher frequencies that active noise cancelling handles less well. It also creates the closed space that the inward-facing microphone needs to measure what your ear actually hears.
keyNumbers: Tip openings typically about 3 to 4 mm across
Ear canals average roughly 7 mm in diameter
Ear canals are about 25 mm long
details.madeOf: Flexible silicone that is easy to wash and resists earwax and oils. Some third-party tips use memory foam instead, which expands to fill the canal for an even tighter seal.

parts.name: Right ear tip

parts.description: Half of the bud that faces your ear, with the sound outlet, a vent and a window for the skin sensor.

details.didYouKnow: The pressure-equalising vent is part of why modern noise-cancelling buds feel less like being underwater than older sealed designs.
details.howItWorks: Inside the right inner shell the inward-facing feedback microphone sits right next to the sound outlet, listening to the sound that actually reaches your ear. Comparing that with what the driver was meant to play lets the processor correct for leaks and for the shape of your ear many times a second. The shell's angled nozzle sets how deep and at what angle the bud sits in your ear.
keyNumbers: Inner microphone sits within a few millimetres of the outlet
Shell moulded to tolerances of about a tenth of a millimetre
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded plastic, finished smooth because it touches skin for long periods. Smooth surfaces are more comfortable and easier to keep clean.

parts.name: Right inner shell

parts.description: Sensor that tells skin from a pocket or a table, so music pauses the moment you take the bud out.

details.didYouKnow: Some earbuds also let you use just one bud while the other charges, swapping them to listen almost continuously all day.
details.howItWorks: Each bud has its own sensor, so the system knows whether you are wearing one, both or neither. If you take only the right bud out, playback can pause or switch to mono in the left, and call audio can move to whichever bud is still in. When both buds are out the system can also lower its power use while waiting to go back in the case.
keyNumbers: Check runs typically several times per second
Detection window only a few millimetres wide
Saves up to hours of battery by sleeping when not worn
details.madeOf: A small sensor chip behind a window in the inner shell, sealed against sweat. The window material is chosen to let the sensor's signal through without spoiling the shell's look.

parts.name: Right skin sensor

parts.description: Tiny microphone in the sound outlet that listens to what's actually reaching your ear, so noise cancelling can correct what it missed.

details.didYouKnow: Listening inside the ear also lets some buds check their own seal: they play a short sound when you put them in and measure how it comes back, then adjust the bass to suit your ear.
details.howItWorks: The outward-facing microphones hear noise before it arrives, but they can't know how the bud is sitting in your ear. This second microphone sits between the speaker and your eardrum and hears what's actually left over. The chip compares it with what it meant to play and corrects the difference many thousands of times a second.
keyNumbers: About the size of a grain of rice or smaller
Part of a correction loop running thousands of times a second
details.madeOf: A MEMS microphone: a tiny silicon membrane etched from a chip, in a small metal can that shields it from radio interference, on a flexible circuit.

parts.name: Right inner microphone

parts.description: Tiny speaker with a light diaphragm and a magnet, pointed straight down the ear canal.

details.didYouKnow: Earbuds can sound bass-heavy despite their tiny drivers because the sealed ear canal acts like a small pressure chamber, where even small movements create big pressure changes.
details.howItWorks: The driver sits facing straight down the nozzle so sound reaches the eardrum with as few reflections as possible. Software equalisation reshapes its output to suit the sealed ear canal and can adapt as the inner microphone measures your fit. When noise cancelling is on, the driver plays an inverted copy of the outside noise so the two waves largely cancel at your eardrum.
keyNumbers: Driver weighs well under 1 g
Can play loud enough to exceed about 100 dB
Anti-noise must arrive within roughly a millisecond of the noise
details.madeOf: A diaphragm of thin plastic film, sometimes with stiffer layers to stop it flexing out of shape, driven by a voice coil and a neodymium magnet. A light, stiff diaphragm moves quickly and accurately for clearer sound.

parts.name: Right speaker driver

parts.description: Folded circuit board with the Bluetooth radio, audio processor and noise-cancelling engine in one package.

details.didYouKnow: Running noise cancelling, sensors and radio on one tiny chip all day uses only a few milliwatts, far less than a single small LED bulb.
details.howItWorks: On most modern buds each side has its own full chip, and the two talk to each other or each listen to the phone directly. The right chip handles its own noise cancelling and plays its own channel of the stereo music, with timing kept matched so both sides stay in step. It can also take over as the main bud if the left is put away.
keyNumbers: Left and right audio kept in sync to within roughly microseconds
Bluetooth LE Audio uses the LC3 codec
Audio delay typically roughly 100 to 200 milliseconds
details.madeOf: A system-in-package that wraps several silicon dies, tiny passive parts and shielding into one sealed module. Putting everything in one package saves space and shortens the wiring, which cuts power use.

parts.name: Right audio chip & board

parts.description: Button-shaped lithium-ion cell that runs the bud for several hours between visits to the case.

details.didYouKnow: Lithium-ion cells age fastest when kept full and warm, so leaving earbuds in a hot car on a full charge wears them out sooner than normal use.
details.howItWorks: Each time the bud goes into the case it is topped up, usually with fast charging that fills the first part of the battery quickly and then slows down to protect the cell near full. Many earbuds also learn your routine and hold the charge at about 80 percent until shortly before you usually take them out. Over hundreds of cycles the cell slowly loses capacity, which is why older buds last less long.
keyNumbers: About 5 minutes in the case gives roughly 1 hour of listening
Typically keeps about 80 percent capacity after roughly 500 cycles
Weighs about 1 g
details.madeOf: A coin-shaped lithium-ion cell in a stainless steel can. The coin shape suits the rounded head of the bud better than the flat pouches used in phones.

parts.name: Right battery

parts.description: Glossy outer half of the bud, with mesh-covered openings for the outward-facing microphones.

details.didYouKnow: Transparency mode has to work very fast; if the played-back sound arrived even slightly late, it would mix with the real sound leaking past the tip and sound echoey.
details.howItWorks: The right outer shell mirrors the left, holding its own outward microphone that also powers transparency mode. In that mode the processor plays outside sound back through the driver, adjusting it so voices sound natural, as if you were not wearing earbuds at all. Its smooth surface helps cut the hiss and rumble of wind hitting the microphone openings.
keyNumbers: Typically 2 microphone openings on the outer face
Transparency mode adds a delay of only roughly milliseconds
Shell outer surface only a few square centimetres
details.madeOf: Durable plastic with a coating that resists scratches and skin oils. A light colour or gloss finish helps hide the small scuffs from daily handling.

parts.name: Right outer shell

parts.description: Acoustic mesh over the microphone that listens to outside noise for noise cancelling and transparency mode.

details.didYouKnow: Noise cancelling is very good on steady sounds like aeroplane engines and much weaker on sudden or high-pitched sounds, which is why you can still hear voices and keyboard clicks.
details.howItWorks: This mesh protects the right feedforward microphone, which samples outside noise for the right ear's noise cancelling. Because noise often arrives at one ear before the other, each bud runs its own cancelling using its own microphones. The mesh's acoustic resistance is matched carefully so the microphone hears the true sound, not a muffled version.
keyNumbers: Typical noise reduction up to about 20 to 30 dB at low frequencies
Mesh typically a few millimetres across
Microphone samples sound tens of thousands of times a second
details.madeOf: Fine stainless steel mesh, sometimes finished in a dark colour to match the shell. Steel resists corrosion from sweat and keeps its shape when cleaned.

parts.name: Right outer microphone mesh

parts.description: Stem that carries the antenna, microphones and the squeeze control, and points the voice mic toward your mouth.

details.didYouKnow: Because each stem has its own voice microphone, calls can continue seamlessly if you take one bud out mid-conversation.
details.howItWorks: Like the left, the right stem houses the antenna, squeeze sensor and voice microphone, but each bud usually has its own full set so either can be used alone. The stem also lines the bud up in the case so its charging contacts land exactly on the pins. Its length gives enough room to keep the antenna away from the metal battery can in the bud's head.
keyNumbers: Bud about 30 mm tall overall
Stem flat face roughly 3 to 5 mm wide
Holds the charging contacts at its very tip
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic, often with internal ribs for stiffness. A stiff stem flexes predictably, which matters for the squeeze sensor to read presses accurately.

parts.name: Right stem

parts.description: Pressure sensor in the flat of the stem: squeeze to play, pause, skip or switch noise modes.

details.didYouKnow: Earbuds play a little click sound in your ear when you squeeze, a trick that makes a solid sensor feel like a real button.
details.howItWorks: The right squeeze sensor works just like the left, and settings often let you give each side its own action, such as noise modes on one and a voice assistant on the other. It ignores the slow, light pressure of your fingers when you adjust the bud and only reacts to a firm, quick press. Swipes along the stem on some buds are detected by a touch-sensing strip beside it to change volume.
keyNumbers: Squeeze area roughly 4 to 5 mm across
Response time roughly a fraction of a second
Long press usually held about 1 second or more
details.madeOf: A thin sensing element on a flex circuit, sealed behind the stem wall with no moving parts. With nothing to wear out, it can survive far more presses than a mechanical button.

parts.name: Right squeeze sensor

parts.description: Thin conductor running down the stem, as far from your head as possible, for a steadier Bluetooth link.

details.didYouKnow: Bluetooth's channel hopping borrows from an idea co-patented in 1942 by actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil.
details.howItWorks: The right antenna links this bud to the phone and to the left bud. Signals passing between the two buds have to travel around or through your head, which absorbs 2.4 GHz energy, so antenna placement in the stem makes a big difference to dropouts. The radio can switch its power and channel many times a second to dodge interference.
keyNumbers: Bluetooth hops between about 40 to 80 channels
Changes channel up to about 1,600 times a second
Transmit power typically only a few milliwatts
details.madeOf: A copper conductor, sometimes formed by laser-plating a pattern straight onto the plastic stem. That method lets the antenna follow the stem's curves without a separate part.

parts.name: Right antenna

parts.description: Microphone at the tip of the stem that picks up your voice for calls, helped by a bone-motion sensor.

details.didYouKnow: Your own voice reaches you partly through the bones of your skull, which is why voice recordings of yourself sound unfamiliar; the bone-motion sensor listens to that same path.
details.howItWorks: The right voice microphone gives the system a second listening point near your mouth, and the buds can pick whichever side has less wind or noise at that moment. A built-in motion sensor feels the tiny vibrations of your jaw and skull when you speak, so the bud can tell your voice apart from someone talking nearby. Processing then lowers the background so the caller hears mostly you.
keyNumbers: Voice mic sits about 3 cm closer to your mouth than the bud head
Accelerometer chip only about 2 mm across
Calls typically sampled at 16 kHz or more
details.madeOf: A silicon MEMS microphone and a small accelerometer, each in tiny metal or plastic packages. Both are made with chip-making techniques, so they are small, cheap and consistent.

parts.name: Right voice microphone

parts.description: Gold-plated contacts at the end of the stem that touch matching pins in the case to charge.

details.didYouKnow: Gold is used on connectors in almost all electronics, from earbuds to spacecraft, because it is one of the few metals that never forms an oxide layer in air.
details.howItWorks: These contacts let the case recharge the right bud and confirm it is seated. They are placed on the very end of the stem so they sit deep in the well, away from your fingers and skin when the bud is worn. The bud's charging circuit controls current through them so the tiny battery is never fed more than it can take.
keyNumbers: Charging voltage about 5 V or less
Contacts each only about 1 mm across
Designed for thousands of in-and-out cycles
details.madeOf: Gold-plated metal pads, flush with the plastic. Gold plating gives low, stable resistance and survives thousands of insertions without wearing through.

parts.name: Right charging contacts

parts.description: Hinged lid held shut by magnets; opening it wakes the buds and pops up the pairing card on a nearby phone.

details.didYouKnow: Many people open and close their earbud case as a fidget habit; the hinge and lid are designed to survive tens of thousands of cycles.
details.howItWorks: When the lid opens, a magnetic sensor on the case board notices the change and the case wakes the buds, which start advertising themselves over Bluetooth. A paired phone nearby can then show the battery levels straight away. Closing the lid puts the buds to sleep and disconnects them so they can charge.
keyNumbers: Lid opens to roughly 90 to 110 degrees
Lid shell about 1 mm thick
Wakes the buds in about a second
details.madeOf: Glossy moulded plastic matching the case body. Plastic keeps the lid light so the hinge spring can flick it open smoothly.

parts.name: Case lid

parts.description: Small stainless-steel hinge with a spring that snaps the lid open or shut past its midpoint.

details.didYouKnow: The over-centre spring idea used in earbud lids is the same principle found in light switches and hair clips: it stores energy until a tipping point, then releases it all at once.
details.howItWorks: The hinge uses a small spring and a shaped cam so the lid has two stable positions, open and shut. Past the midpoint, the spring takes over and finishes the movement, which gives the satisfying snap. It is set into the body so it carries any twisting force on the lid without loosening.
keyNumbers: Pin roughly 1 mm in diameter
Rated for tens of thousands of openings
Hinge assembly typically about 1 cm wide
details.madeOf: Stainless steel pin and spring in a metal or tough plastic housing. Stainless steel resists rust from pocket moisture and keeps its springiness for years.

parts.name: Lid hinge

parts.description: Small magnets that hold the lid shut and pull each bud down onto its charging pins.

details.didYouKnow: Neodymium magnets were developed in the early 1980s and are now in everything from earbuds to electric car motors and wind turbines.
details.howItWorks: A pair of magnets in the lid and body pull the lid shut, and further magnets in the wells grab the steel and magnetic parts in each bud. This pulls the buds down onto the charging pins and stops them falling out if the case is opened upside down. Magnets are also how the case can sense the lid position and snap onto a magnetic wireless charger.
keyNumbers: Typically about 10 or more magnets in the case
Each magnet only a few millimetres long
Neodymium magnets can hold roughly 1,000 times their own weight
details.madeOf: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets, often nickel-plated to stop corrosion. Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets widely available, so tiny ones are enough.

parts.name: Magnets

parts.description: Moulded insert with a shaped pocket for each bud, so a bud can only drop in one way, with its contacts on the pins.

details.didYouKnow: A left bud won't fit the right pocket. The shape is doing the job a label would otherwise do, and it means the case always knows which bud is which.
details.howItWorks: Each pocket is shaped to the bud, with a deep channel for the stem and a wider cup for the head. Because the shape only fits one way, a bud dropped in lands with its contacts squarely on the pins. Magnets do the final bit of pulling, which is why buds seem to snap into place.
keyNumbers: Built to tolerances of a fraction of a millimetre
Holds the buds within a few millimetres of the wireless coil and battery
details.madeOf: Usually an injection-moulded plastic insert, smooth enough for a bud to slide in easily. It's designed so the pockets can be wiped clean of ear wax and pocket lint.

parts.name: Bud wells

parts.description: Moulded plastic shell with two shaped wells that each hold an earbud in exactly the right spot.

details.didYouKnow: The outline of the earbud wells must allow for the ear tips too, which is why only certain third-party tips fit in the case with the lid closed.
details.howItWorks: The body holds everything together: the battery, board, coil, speaker and port sit beneath the two wells. Each well is shaped so a bud can only go in one way, guiding the stem's contacts onto the pins. The rounded outer shape fits comfortably in a pocket and spreads the force if the case is dropped.
keyNumbers: Case about 60 x 45 x 22 mm
Weighs about 50 g with buds inside
Wells moulded to fractions of a millimetre
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded polycarbonate, sometimes with an internal metal or plastic frame. Polycarbonate is tough, takes a glossy finish and lets wireless charging and radio signals pass through.

parts.name: Case body

parts.description: Small light on the front that shows the charge level and pairing status.

details.didYouKnow: Blue LEDs were so hard to make that the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics went to the researchers who cracked it, which in turn made white and full-colour LEDs possible.
details.howItWorks: A small multicolour LED shines through a tiny hole or a thin section of plastic on the front of the case. Its colour typically shows the charge level, for example green when well charged and amber when low or charging, and it flashes white when the buds are ready to pair. The case board controls it and switches it off quickly to save battery.
keyNumbers: LED chip roughly 1 mm across
Draws only a few milliamps
Usually lights for a few seconds at a time
details.madeOf: A tiny semiconductor chip containing red, green and blue light-emitting junctions, under a clear plastic light pipe. LEDs give bright, low-power light from a chip smaller than a grain of rice.

parts.name: Status light

parts.description: Lithium-ion cell several times larger than both bud batteries together, good for about four more full charges.

details.didYouKnow: The case battery holds about ten times as much energy as one earbud, but is still several times smaller than a typical phone battery.
details.howItWorks: The case battery is a reservoir that refills the bud batteries whenever they are docked. Its charging circuit raises its voltage slightly to push current into the buds, losing a little energy as heat each time. Because the case does not run any power-hungry parts most of the time, it can sit unused for weeks and still have charge left.
keyNumbers: Capacity roughly 400 to 600 mAh
Gives about 4 extra full charges for the buds
Around 30 hours of total listening with the buds
details.madeOf: A lithium-ion pouch or prismatic cell, much larger than the buds' coin cells, wrapped in an insulating film. A flat cell fits neatly under the wells in the base.

parts.name: Case battery

parts.description: Flat copper coil behind the back wall that lets the case charge on a wireless pad, with a magnet ring to align it.

details.didYouKnow: The Qi wireless charging standard was launched around 2010 by the Wireless Power Consortium, and the name comes from the Chinese word for life energy.
details.howItWorks: The coil sits flat against the back wall. When the case is placed on a wireless charger, a changing magnetic field from the charger's coil induces a current in this one, which the board rectifies to charge the battery. A ring of magnets around it can snap the case into perfect alignment on magnetic chargers, which makes charging faster and cooler.
keyNumbers: Works at roughly 100 to 200 kHz
Wireless charging typically up to about 5 W for earbud cases
Coil about 2 to 3 cm across
details.madeOf: Many turns of thin copper wire, often twisted multi-strand wire, laid over a ferrite sheet. The ferrite steers the magnetic field and shields the battery and electronics behind it.

parts.name: Wireless charging coil

parts.description: Board in the base that manages charging, talks to the buds and runs the case's own tracking radio.

details.didYouKnow: Some modern cases can be located even when no paired phone is nearby, by quietly passing their encrypted location through strangers' phones that happen to walk past.
details.howItWorks: The case board decides where power goes: from the USB-C port or wireless coil into the case battery, and from the battery out to each bud. It reads the lid sensor, reports battery levels to the buds and phone, and drives the LED and speaker. On many recent cases it also has its own low-energy radio so a lost case can be found by nearby phones.
keyNumbers: Board typically about 3 to 4 cm long
Bluetooth Low Energy uses about 40 channels
Battery level usually reported in steps of about 1 to 10 percent
details.madeOf: A small multilayer circuit board with a microcontroller, charging and protection chips and a Bluetooth radio. Fibreglass board material is stiff, insulating and cheap to make in large numbers.

parts.name: Case circuit board

parts.description: Spring-loaded gold pins at the bottom of each well that press against the contacts on the end of a stem.

details.didYouKnow: Gold plating here is usually a tiny fraction of a micrometre to a few micrometres thick. It's the surface that matters, because sweat and skin oils quickly dull most other metals.
details.howItWorks: Each pin sits on a tiny spring, so it presses firmly against the contact on the end of a stem even if the bud isn't seated perfectly. Besides power, the same contacts usually carry data, so the case can read a bud's battery level and hand over pairing information.
keyNumbers: Spring travel of around a millimetre or less
Rated for many thousands of cycles
Charges a bud in well under an hour
details.madeOf: Brass or similar pins plated with gold, which doesn't corrode and keeps its low resistance after thousands of insertions, mounted in a plastic block on a flexible circuit.

parts.name: Charging pins

parts.description: Tiny speaker that chirps so you can find a lost case, and confirms when charging starts.

details.didYouKnow: The human ear is most sensitive between about 2 and 5 kHz, which is why alarm and locator tones are often tuned to that range.
details.howItWorks: The speaker is a tiny driver tucked into the base and pointed at a small grille. It plays a chime when charging starts or the case is low, and a loud tone when you ask your phone to find the case. The sound is tuned to high, piercing frequencies because they are easier to locate under sofa cushions.
keyNumbers: Speaker only about 1 cm across
Tones typically pitched at a few kilohertz
Can sound for up to minutes when locating the case
details.madeOf: A small piezo or dynamic speaker with a plastic or metal diaphragm. Small speakers are most efficient at high pitches, which suits find-my beeps perfectly.

parts.name: Case speaker

parts.description: Reversible charging port in the bottom of the case.

details.didYouKnow: USB-C was introduced in 2014, and the European Union later made it the required charging port for many small electronic devices, including earbuds.
details.howItWorks: The USB-C port takes power from a cable and passes it to the case board, which charges the case battery and then the buds. Its symmetrical design means the plug works either way up. The case uses only a small part of what USB-C can deliver, so almost any phone or laptop charger will work.
keyNumbers: Connector has 24 pins
Port opening about 8.4 x 2.6 mm
Rated for about 10,000 insertions
details.madeOf: A stainless steel shell around a plastic tongue with gold-plated contacts, soldered and anchored to the board. The steel shell takes the strain of plugging and unplugging.

parts.name: USB-C port

parts.description: Steel loop on the side of the case for a wrist strap.

details.didYouKnow: Lanyard loops on small gadgets date back to early mobile phones and cameras, when wrist straps were a popular way to avoid drops.
details.howItWorks: The loop is anchored into the case body so a wrist strap or keyring cord can pass through it. It is fixed into the internal frame, not just the outer plastic, so a tug on the strap does not crack the shell. Its side position keeps the strap clear of the lid, the port and the wireless charging face.
keyNumbers: Loop opening roughly 2 to 3 mm wide
Adds well under 1 g to the case
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, polished or finished to match the case. Steel is strong in a very small cross-section and does not wear thin from the rubbing of a cord.

parts.name: Lanyard loop

summary: Noise-cancelling wireless earbuds and their charging case: each bud is a tiny computer with a speaker, microphones, a battery and a radio, and the case is a pocket battery that recharges them.
